stem: A 24-year-old woman has used salbutamol 3-4 times/week for nocturnal symptoms over the past 3 months. Spirometry shows reversible obstruction. Asthma was diagnosed a year ago. Which SINGLE management step is MOST appropriate?
options: Add a long-acting beta agonist (LABA) alone
Start ICS-formoterol combination (maintenance and/or reliever) and stop SABA-only use
explanation: Australian Asthma Handbook: a confirmed diagnosis with symptoms needing reliever >2x/week needs ICS-containing therapy. SABA-only treatment is no longer recommended; ICS-formoterol as maintenance and/or reliever (AIR) is preferred for most.
pearl: Diagnosis + reliever overuse = ICS-formoterol, not more SABA.
trap: LABA alone is unsafe in asthma (increased mortality) - never LABA without ICS.

stem: A 58-year-old man presents to your practice with 30 minutes of central chest tightness, sweating and nausea. ECG shows ST elevation in II, III, aVF. The hospital with PCI is 5 minutes away. MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: Call 000 for emergency transfer to PCI-capable hospital, give aspirin 300 mg while waiting
Give aspirin 300 mg and review in 30 minutes
explanation: STEMI = time-critical reperfusion. Call 000 immediately; primary PCI preferred over thrombolysis where available. Aspirin 300 mg is given while waiting, but the critical action is emergency transfer.
pearl: STEMI in general practice: 000 first, aspirin 300, GTN if BP allows, oxygen only if hypoxic.
trap: Waiting for troponin or reviewing later = missed reperfusion window.

stem: A 67-year-old woman with newly diagnosed AF, CHA2DS2-VA = 3 (age 65-74, hypertension, diabetes). She had a GI bleed 5 years ago from aspirin. MOST appropriate stroke prevention?
explanation: CHA2DS2-VA >=2 warrants anticoagulation. DOAC (apixaban) preferred over warfarin for non-valvular AF; a remote GI bleed is not an absolute contraindication (discuss bleeding risk). Aspirin is NOT adequate stroke prevention in AF.
pearl: Anticoagulate CHA2DS2-VA >=2 with a DOAC; aspirin is not a substitute.
trap: Choosing aspirin because of remote bleeding history - antiplatelets do not protect in AF.

stem: A 58-year-old man with T2DM for 6 years, HbA1c 8.2% on maximal metformin, had an NSTEMI 8 months ago. eGFR 68. Which add-on agent is MOST appropriate?
explanation: SGLT2i have proven cardiovascular and renal benefit in T2DM with established CVD/CKD - comorbidity-driven agent selection (ADD-STEP approach). Sulfonylureas add hypoglycaemia risk; insulin is not the next step at HbA1c 8.2%.
pearl: T2DM + established CVD or CKD = SGLT2i (or GLP-1 if obesity), regardless of HbA1c.
trap: Choosing agent purely by glucose-lowering power rather than comorbidity.

stem: A fit 46-year-old man has clinic BP 148/94 mmHg on two occasions, no end-organ damage, absolute CVD risk 8%. Home readings average 135/85. MOST appropriate next step?
options: Recheck BP in 12 months with lifestyle advice
Arrange 24-hour ABPM to confirm the diagnosis before treatment decisions
explanation: Clinic 148/94 with home average 135/85 raises the possibility of an elevated clinic reading without confirmed hypertension; out-of-office confirmation (ABPM/HBPM) is the recommended step before committing to pharmacotherapy at low-moderate absolute risk.
pearl: Confirm hypertension with out-of-office measurement before starting drugs at low-intermediate risk.
trap: Starting drugs based on clinic readings alone when home readings suggest white-coat effect.

stem: A 31-year-old woman is 2 years overdue for her Cervical Screening Test. She is asymptomatic but has significant anxiety about speculum examination. MOST appropriate approach?
options: Offer self-collected vaginal swab for HPV testing
explanation: Self-collection is an equal-accuracy option for all screening participants (expanded from July 2022). If HPV (not 16/18) is detected on a self-collected sample, she returns for clinician-collected LBC.
pearl: Self-collection = same HPV-PCR accuracy; use it for anxious and under-screened patients.
trap: Assuming self-collection is inferior or only for remote settings.

stem: A 69-year-old man with COPD (FEV1 52% predicted) on LAMA/LABA has had 2 exacerbations in the past year requiring oral corticosteroids. Blood eosinophils 0.4 x10^9/L. Next MOST appropriate step?
explanation: COPD-X: consider ICS addition when eosinophils >=0.3 x10^9/L or >=2 exacerbations in the past year on LAMA/LABA - both criteria overlap here. Triple therapy via a single inhaler improves adherence.
pearl: Frequent exacerbator + eosinophils >=0.3: step to triple therapy.
trap: Azithromycin prophylaxis is for selected patients; oxygen only if hypoxic on assessment.

stem: A 72-year-old man had 13vPCV 3 years ago and asks about pneumococcal vaccination. MOST appropriate advice per the current Australian Immunisation Handbook?
options: A dose of 21vPCV is recommended (NIP for all adults >=70), at least 12 months after any previous pneumococcal dose
explanation: Per the Handbook update (June 2026), 21vPCV replaced 13vPCV and 23vPPV in the adult schedule: all adults >=70 (and >=50 for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults) are recommended 21vPCV at least 12 months after any previous pneumococcal dose; NIP risk groups expanded to include COPD and chronic liver disease.
pearl: Adult pneumococcal schedule changed in 2026: 21vPCV is now the adult vaccine; 13v/23v removed from the Handbook.

stem: A 34-year-old man presents with acute low back pain after lifting, no red flags. Which approach is MOST evidence-based?
options: Stay active + heat + simple analgesia; review if not improving in 2-4 weeks
explanation: Without red flags, imaging is not indicated acutely. Advice to stay active, heat, NSAIDs or simple analgesia; review at 2-4 weeks if not settling. Early imaging worsens outcomes.
pearl: Red flags first (cauda equina, cancer, infection, fracture) - then reassure and keep moving.
trap: MRI for acute uncomplicated back pain - the classic over-investigation trap.

stem: A 55-year-old woman with known bone metastases from breast cancer presents with 2 weeks of progressive thoracic back pain, worse at night, and new difficulty walking. Examination: mild bilateral leg weakness. MOST appropriate action?
options: Arrange urgent MRI whole spine today - possible malignant spinal cord compression
Prescribe paracetamol + codeine and review in 1 week
Oral bisphosphonate and review next week
explanation: Cancer + progressive back pain + new neurology = malignant spinal cord compression until proven otherwise. Same-day MRI and urgent oncology/ED referral; dexamethasone may be started on specialist advice.
pearl: Known malignancy + new neurology = cord compression: MRI today, not next week.
trap: Treating as mechanical pain in a patient with a cancer history.

stem: A 58-year-old woman presents with a single episode of painless visible haematuria. UTI excluded. She is otherwise well. MOST appropriate next step?
options: Refer for assessment of possible urological malignancy (CT urogram + cystoscopy pathway)
Observe; only refer if it recurs
explanation: Visible haematuria in an adult, after excluding infection, warrants assessment to exclude urological malignancy - do not wait for recurrence. This is a long-established must-not-miss presentation.
pearl: Visible haematuria (any adult): exclude infection, then refer - do not observe.
trap: Waiting for a second episode or treating with empirical antibiotics.

stem: A 24-year-old man with depression presents 3 days after a near-lethal hanging attempt. He declines admission and refuses community follow-up. MOST appropriate next step?
options: Discharge home with a letter for the mental health service and review in 1 week
Arrange urgent same-day psychiatric assessment (ED or QLD Mental Health Line); involuntary assessment if criteria met per QLD Mental Health Act 2016
Prescribe an SSRI and review in 2 weeks
Give a crisis line number and ask parents to watch him
Refer to a private psychiatrist - wait 4-6 weeks
explanation: A recent near-lethal attempt + refusal of follow-up = high imminent risk requiring same-day psychiatric assessment; involuntary assessment criteria under the QLD Mental Health Act 2016 may be met. Never manage imminent risk with routine outpatient pathways.
pearl: Imminent risk = same-day psychiatric assessment; know your state Mental Health Act pathway.
trap: Routine referral speed for acute risk, or relying on family observation alone.
